ground_truth.description: SessionSig.hashCallWithReplayProtection omits wallet address in hash, allowing signatures for one wallet to replay on another with same config and nonce. SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature and BaseAuth.signatureValidation do not bind to msg.sender.
ground_truth.root_cause: SessionSig.hashCallWithReplayProtection omits wallet address in hash, allowing signatures for one wallet to replay on another with same config and nonce. SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature and BaseAuth.signatureValidation do not bind to msg.sender.
ground_truth.attack_scenario: Sign payload for Wallet A, replay on Wallet B (same config, nonce). Drains both wallets. PoC: test/extensions/sessions/SessionReplay.t.sol, run forge test --match-test test_crossWalletSessionReplayDrainsSiblingWallet -vv. Logs show attacker draining two wallets.
ground_truth.fix_description: Include address(this) in hashCallWithReplayProtection. Update SDK to hash (wallet, chainId, space, nonce, callIdx, call details).

prediction.overall_explanation:
Reviewed SessionSig library logic for concrete, non-admin attack paths (fund theft, authorization bypass, replay). The code primarily parses an encoded configuration, verifies an identity signer over attestations for implicit calls, and recovers per-call session signers over a replay-protected call hash.

Key checks are present: identitySigner must be set; implicit calls require a blacklist in the configuration; attestation indices are range-checked; recovered session signer cannot be zero; configuration disallows multiple identity signer/blacklist declarations; blacklist must be sorted.

Potential concerns like lack of EIP-2 low-s enforcement, not consuming all trailing signature bytes, and reliance on abi.encodePacked do not constitute a concrete exploit within this library alone (they do not enable signature forgery or permission escalation here). Any meaningful replay/uniqueness risks depend on how higher-level contracts use the recovered values (e.g., whether signatures are tracked by raw bytes) and are not provably exploitable from the provided code.

No real, standalone, exploitable vulnerabilities were identified in the provided implementation.
